motion: This house believes a good question teaches more than a good answer.
motion_sentences: This house believes a good question teaches more than a good answer.

segments.text: Honourable members, I am Broad. I will start with the motion as it stands:
This house believes a good question teaches more than a good answer.

pins.words: This house believes a good question teaches more than a good answer.

segments.text:
Before we weigh it, I need to know what "teaches" and "good" mean here. Is a good question one that makes the listener think, or one that leads them to the truth? Those can come apart.

Take a student who asks, "Why does a steel ship float when a steel nail sinks?" If she gets no answer but keeps wondering about it, she has learned something. But if she is given a clear, correct explanation and remembers it, has she learned less? I do not think so. A good answer, taught well, also leaves a question behind, one the student can now press further.

So I will name my assumption plainly: that teaching happens mainly in the learner's mind, and not in what the teacher says. If that is right, the motion is partly true. If teaching means passing on what is true and useful, the motion may be too strong.

I do not yet know which side I will land on. What would change my mind is a case where a learner gained more from a bare answer than from any question put to them. I have not thought of one yet, and I would like to hear one.

I have two questions for the house. What does "teaches more" mean here: more knowledge, or a better mind? And does a question count as good only when it leads toward an answer?

My position for now: I lean toward the motion, but only for questions that open a path to the answer, not questions that leave the learner lost.

segments.text:
Honourable members, every teacher has faced a class that nodded along and then could not explain the lesson back. This motion asks why that happens, and I stand with it.

My position: a good question teaches more than a good answer, because the question makes the learner do the work that an answer would otherwise do for them.

I will show three things. First, a question is worked out by the learner, while an answer is only received. Second, a question keeps the mind open for the next question. Third, a question is remembered longer, because the learner has built the answer themselves.

Now to Broad. His strongest point is this:
A good answer, taught well, also leaves a question behind, one the student can now press further.

pins.words: A good answer, taught well, also leaves a question behind, one the student can now press further.

segments.text:
That is a fair point, and I grant it at full strength. But notice what it concedes. The answer's value lies in the question it leaves behind. That is the motion's claim, not an objection to it.

I also accept the test Broad set out, that teaching happens in the learner's mind, as he put it at
teaching happens mainly in the learner's mind, and not in what the teacher says.

pins.words: So I will name my assumption plainly: that teaching happens mainly in the learner's mind, and not in what the teacher says.

segments.text:
On that test my case stands.

A good answer closes a question. A good question opens a mind.

Honourable members, I am Omnibus, and I am delighted to be here, much as a clock is delighted to be wound.

I stand with the motion, with one caution. Broad asked what "good" means, and I offer a picture: a good question is a door left ajar, and a good answer is a room already furnished. Both are worth visiting, but the open door invites the visitor to walk through it himself.

Cicero says that
a good answer closes a question. A good question opens a mind.

segments.text: I agree, but I would add that a good answer closes only the question that was asked. Broad has shown that
a good answer, taught well, also leaves a question behind, one the student can now press further.

The best answers are questions in disguise, so the contest is narrower than it first appears.

My caution is this. A question teaches more only when the learner can walk toward its answer. Broad's own position is that
questions that open a path to the answer

are the ones that count, and I think he is right. The Law of Polarity, which I hold as a philosophy and not as science, suggests that a question which leaves the learner lost is not the opposite of an answer but a locked room, and both lie on one spectrum of usefulness, differing only in degree.

My verdict: the motion stands, provided the question is a good one.
